The Value Metric, Under Pressure

What the unit of charge does to a company once real money, real customers and real marginal cost are attached to it.

This reading assumes the working knowledge: that a value metric is the unit a price is attached to, that it should track what the customer actually receives, and that a candidate metric must be alignable, meterable, forecastable and reasonably hard to game. That material is not repeated here. What follows takes the idea into the territory where competent practitioners stop agreeing with one another — where the metric collides with cost of goods, with revenue recognition, with the sales compensation plan, with a regulator, and with a customer base whose usage is distributed as a power law rather than a bell curve.

1. Two decisions, six weeks apart

On the morning of 14 January 2026, in a glass-walled room on the fourth floor of an office park off Bengaluru's Outer Ring Road, Sharanya Iyer laid three printouts face-down on the table before turning any of them over. She was the chief product officer of Nishkarsh Systems, a seven-year-old company that sold data-reliability software: the layer that watched an enterprise's data pipelines and told a bank, an insurer or a retailer when a nightly load had silently dropped a fifth of its rows. Nishkarsh had 214 paying accounts across India, Singapore and the Gulf, annual recurring revenue of ₹186 crore, and a pricing model that had been designed in 2019 by two engineers and a spreadsheet: ₹4,200 per monitored table per month, with volume discounts that kicked in at 500, 2,000 and 10,000 tables.

The first printout was a renewal. Nishkarsh's second-largest account, a private-sector insurer in Mumbai, had migrated its warehouse onto a lakehouse architecture over the previous year. In doing so, its data engineering group had consolidated 11,400 monitored tables into 1,900 wide, partitioned ones. The volume of data under observation had risen by roughly forty percent. The number of incidents Nishkarsh detected and routed had risen by sixty-one percent. The contract value, calculated strictly per the signed schedule, was going to fall from ₹4.1 crore to ₹87 lakh. Nobody had cheated. The insurer's head of data platforms had, in a call the previous week, been genuinely apologetic and entirely unmoved: "We did the right engineering thing. Your commercial model punished you for it. That is not a problem I can solve."

The second printout was a cohort analysis her pricing lead, Faisal Rahman, had run over the Christmas break. Across the 214 accounts, table counts had grown at a median of four percent a year since 2022. Rows processed had grown at thirty-one percent. Incidents detected had grown at twenty-six percent. The metric Nishkarsh billed on was, empirically, the only quantity in the business that was not growing. The third printout was from Meera Vaidyanathan, the chief financial officer, and it was a single page: if Nishkarsh moved to a consumption metric, roughly ₹52 crore of currently committed annual revenue would convert from fixed subscription to variable consideration under Ind AS 115, which meant it could no longer be recognised rateably on signature but only as consumed — and the company's reported net revenue retention, the number three prospective investors had been tracking quarterly, would become a function of customer behaviour rather than of contract structure. Meera's covering note read, in its entirety: "I am not against this. I want you to know what you are also deciding."

Six weeks later and 560 kilometres away, on 25 February 2026, Aditya Shenoy was having a different argument about the same thing. Shenoy had co-founded Nitara AI in Pune in 2023 to do contract review, and for two years the product had behaved like software: a lawyer uploaded a master services agreement, Nitara marked up the deviations from the client's playbook, and Nitara charged ₹32,000 per named legal user per month. Eleven months earlier the company had shipped an obligation-tracking agent that read the whole executed contract estate of a client, extracted every dated obligation, monitored the client's own systems for compliance, and raised a flag when a delivery milestone or an indemnity cap or a data-localisation covenant was about to be breached. It worked well. It also ran, continuously, without anyone logging in.

Nitara's largest client, a Chennai-headquartered engineering conglomerate, had nine named users. It had 46,000 live contracts and roughly 310,000 tracked obligations. In January the agent had consumed ₹19.4 lakh of inference. The client had paid ₹2.88 lakh. Shenoy's head of engineering had shown him a chart in which the two lines crossed in the second week of July 2025 and had not been in the same postcode since. "We have a product," she said, "whose best customers we cannot afford." The question on Shenoy's table was not whether to change the metric. It was which of four candidate metrics — documents ingested, obligations under management, agent actions taken, or breaches averted — would survive first contact with a general counsel's procurement team, an inference bill that fell forty percent every nine months, and a competitor who had just announced per-seat pricing at half Nitara's list.

These two decisions look like the same decision and are not. Sharanya's problem is that a correct metric has decayed; Aditya's is that no metric exists yet for a product whose unit of work has no established commercial name. Holding both in view at once is the fastest way to see what the concept of a value metric can and cannot do.

2. The idea, its history, and the four positions people actually hold

Begin with a definition tight enough to argue with. A value metric is the argument of the pricing function: the variable q in a bill B = f(q), chosen such that a customer's own assessment of benefit received is monotonically increasing in q. Three things follow from stating it that way. First, the choice of q is logically prior to the choice of f, which is why packaging, tiering and discounting are all downstream topics. Second, q need not be a single scalar; real pricing functions frequently take two or three arguments, and the discipline of pretending otherwise causes much of the confusion in the field. Third, and least remarked, the definition contains a claim about whose assessment counts. A metric that tracks value as the vendor measures it, but not as the buyer's finance function measures it, will fail at renewal no matter how defensible the underlying economics.

The intellectual history is older than software and is worth knowing precisely, because two of the four schools of thought below take their authority from different parts of it.

The commercial origin is usually dated to Xerox in 1959. The 914 copier cost far more to manufacture than the office-equipment market would pay as a purchase price, and Xerox's response was to retain ownership, install the machine, and charge roughly four cents a copy above a small monthly minimum. The unit of charge became the unit of output. What made the arrangement famous was not the cleverness of the tariff but its consequence: because Xerox's revenue rose with copies, and copies rose with how useful the machine was, Xerox's incentive to make the machine reliable was structural rather than contractual. Rolls-Royce built the same logic into aero-engine support with its "power by the hour" arrangements from the early 1960s, in which airlines paid per flying hour rather than for parts and labour; Michelin later experimented with selling truck tyres by the kilometre. In each case the value metric was the mechanism by which a supplier converted itself from a seller of things into a participant in the buyer's output.

The formal economics arrived from a different direction and with different intentions. Walter Oi's 1971 paper on two-part tariffs — framed, memorably, as the problem of how a monopolist amusement park should split its revenue between the gate and the rides — established that a fixed fee plus a per-unit charge can extract more surplus than either alone, and that the optimal split depends on how heterogeneous the customers are. Mussa and Rosen in 1978 and Maskin and Riley in 1984 developed the screening view: when a seller cannot observe a buyer's type, the price schedule itself is the instrument that sorts buyers, and the "metric" is chosen for its correlation with willingness to pay, not for its correlation with value delivered. Robert Wilson's Nonlinear Pricing (1993) is the standard reference for the resulting machinery. Shapiro and Varian's Information Rules (1999) brought versioning into general management vocabulary. The management-consulting tradition — Nagle and Holden, Hermann Simon, and the McKinsey pricing group whose The Price Advantage (2004) gave the term "price metric" wide currency — then blended the two, and Ramanujam and Tacke's Monetizing Innovation (2016) pushed the resulting practice into product organisations by insisting that the monetisation model be designed before the product, not after.

Out of that history four positions have crystallised. They are usually not stated as positions, which is why disagreements between their adherents feel like disagreements about facts.

3. Mechanics in depth: the arithmetic experts actually run

The working-level treatment of this topic stops at a checklist. What separates an expert is that the checklist has been replaced by four quantities that can be computed from data a company already has, and that trade off against one another in a way a checklist conceals.

3.1 Pass-through, or the alignment coefficient

Define the pass-through coefficient β as the elasticity of the customer's bill with respect to the customer's own value received: β = Δln(revenue per account) / Δln(value proxy per account), estimated across the customer base over a period long enough to contain real growth — eighteen to twenty-four months is the usual window. The value proxy is whatever the customer's own management uses to describe their throughput: policies written, orders shipped, patients treated, contracts executed.

A pure seat model in a product whose value scales with output has β close to zero. A pure consumption model on a well-chosen unit has β near one. Hybrid models sit between. Two consequences follow immediately, and neither is obvious.

The first is that net revenue retention, the metric boards actually watch, is largely an arithmetic property of β rather than a measure of customer-success competence. To a first approximation, for a base whose customers' underlying businesses grow at rate g with gross logo churn c and contraction d, net revenue retention is roughly (1 + βg)(1 − c − d). With g = 26%, as at Nishkarsh, a move from β ≈ 0.15 to β ≈ 0.75 is worth about sixteen percentage points of net revenue retention before a single customer-success conversation has taken place. Companies that hire a fourth customer-success manager to chase what is in fact a metric problem are common enough that the pattern deserves a name.

The second consequence is that β greater than one is not a triumph. A metric that makes the bill grow faster than the customer's benefit — because it is denominated in an input the customer must buy more of as they grow, rather than an output they get more of — produces superb expansion revenue for two years and a renewal cliff in the third. The tell is expansion concentrated in accounts whose satisfaction scores are flat or falling.

3.2 Dispersion, or what the distribution of the metric does to the business

The second quantity is dispersion: the coefficient of variation of the metric across the customer base, and more importantly its concentration. Usage metrics in software are almost always power-law distributed. At Nishkarsh, rows processed had a top-decile share of sixty-eight percent; tables monitored had a top-decile share of thirty-one percent. This matters in three distinct ways that teams routinely conflate.

It matters for revenue risk: a metric with high concentration converts a small number of customer-side events — one migration, one divestment, one internal cost-cutting drive — into large revenue swings. It matters for price-level setting: under a concentrated metric the same list price produces wildly different effective rates, so a single per-unit price will overcharge the head and undercharge the tail unless the tariff is made nonlinear. And it matters for sales compensation, because a metric whose value is concentrated in a few accounts makes territory design, quota setting and commission accrual substantially harder, which is the real, unspoken source of most sales-side resistance to consumption pricing.

3.3 The tariff: getting from a metric to a bill

Choosing q does not produce a price. The step usually left implicit is the design of f(q), and the standard shape in enterprise software is a three-part tariff: a platform fee F, an included allowance q₀, and an overage rate p above the allowance, so that B = F + p · max(0, q − q₀). This shape is not an accident of convention; it is the compromise the four schools can all live with. The platform fee buys legibility and floors the vendor's revenue. The allowance converts most customers into a flat-fee experience, which the behavioural literature on flat-rate bias suggests they will pay a premium for. The overage restores alignment at the margin where the customer is genuinely getting more.

Work the numbers for Nishkarsh's proposed switch. Faisal modelled a metric of "rows scanned per month, in billions", with a platform fee that varied by tier, an included allowance, and an overage rate of ₹680 per billion rows.

The insurer's bill under this structure is ₹8.0 lakh plus 222 billion rows of overage at ₹680, or ₹23.1 lakh a month — ₹2.77 crore a year against the ₹87 lakh the table-based schedule would have produced and the ₹4.1 crore of the expiring contract. That last comparison is the one Sharanya could not avoid. A metric change that is correct in principle still produced, for her most important account, a thirty-two percent reduction against the incumbent contract. Experts are not surprised by this. A decayed metric has usually been propping up price levels that the new metric, honestly applied, will not reproduce, and the choice is between recovering the level through the tariff's parameters — raising F, lowering q₀ — and accepting a one-time reset in exchange for a base that grows on its own thereafter. Conflating those two choices is how metric migrations turn into price rises wearing a disguise, which customers detect quickly and resent durably.

3.4 Cost coupling, and why it changed

The fourth quantity is the correlation between the metric and the vendor's own cost to serve. For two decades this was a rounding error in software: marginal cost per unit of anything was near zero, so any metric was as good as any other on this dimension, and the entire literature could safely treat cost as irrelevant to pricing. Inference costs ended that. The relevant quantity is the contribution margin per unit of the metric, and the relevant question is whether it stays positive across the whole observed distribution of usage.

At Nitara, this is the entire problem. Aditya's four candidate metrics differ enormously in how tightly they are coupled to the cost of the agent's work. Seats are uncoupled: cost per seat ranged from ₹1,100 to ₹2.16 lakh a month across Nitara's base, a factor of nearly two hundred. Documents ingested are partly coupled, because ingestion is a one-time cost and monitoring is recurring. Obligations under management is well coupled, because each obligation is re-evaluated on a schedule. Breaches averted is entirely uncoupled and, worse, inversely related: the better the agent gets, the fewer breaches occur, so revenue falls as quality rises, which is a value metric that punishes its own product for working.

4. When the idea applies, stated as testable claims

The concept is not universally applicable, and the conditions under which it holds can be written as claims that can be checked against data rather than asserted. Four of them do most of the work.

Claim one: value is continuous in the unit, not a step function. The test is whether customer-reported benefit rises materially between the twentieth and eightieth percentile of the metric's distribution. At Nishkarsh this holds strongly for rows scanned — an insurer watching four times the data genuinely gets four times the coverage — and holds weakly for tables. At Nitara it holds for obligations and fails for documents, because a contract that is ingested and never triggers anything delivers little beyond the initial review. Where the claim fails, per-unit pricing manufactures the appearance of rigour on top of a discontinuity, and the honest answer is a flat fee with usage tracked but not billed.

Claim two: the buyer's own management already counts the unit. The test is whether the number appears unprompted in the buyer's internal reporting. This is the single most underrated screen. A metric the buyer already tracks needs no education, survives personnel changes on the customer side, and cannot be disputed at invoice time, because the buyer has an independent source of truth. Rows scanned fails this test at Nishkarsh — no insurer's operating committee reviews row counts — which is precisely why Faisal's model needed a customer-visible meter, a point taken up in section five. Obligations under management passes it at Nitara only after the first year, because the client's legal department begins reporting the number to its own audit committee once Nitara has extracted it.

Claim three: the vendor can meter the unit more cheaply than it can dispute it. The test is the ratio of metering and reconciliation cost, including the loaded cost of support time spent on billing queries and the value of credit notes issued, to the incremental revenue the precision buys. Companies almost never compute this and it is frequently larger than the gain. The practical consequence is that mature companies choose a metric one or two levels coarser than the true driver of value: not seconds but credits, not rows but billions of rows, not agent actions but monthly active obligations.

Claim four: the unit cannot be reduced without reducing benefit. The test is adversarial and should be run as one: give a bright analyst an afternoon, the contract, and the instruction to halve the bill without changing what the business does. The Mumbai insurer's lakehouse migration was not an attack, but it produced exactly the outcome an attack would have produced, which is the more important observation. Gameability and technical evolution are the same risk seen from two angles, and a metric denominated in an implementation detail — tables, servers, environments, endpoints, index shards — is exposed to both.

Where the idea is actively misleading is worth naming explicitly. In products whose value is insurance-like — the compliance tool that prevents one catastrophic fine, the disaster-recovery system, the security control that matters only on the day it matters — the expected value is high and the realised usage is near zero, and any usage-denominated metric will bill close to nothing precisely when the product is working. In products sold into fixed budget lines, such as a government department with a sanctioned annual outlay, a variable bill is not merely unpopular but administratively unusable. And in the early life of any product, the search for a defensible value metric can crowd out the more urgent question of whether anyone will pay anything at all; a founder who spends six weeks perfecting a metric for a product with four customers has confused rigour with progress.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Multi-product estates and the credit currency

Once a company sells three or four products with genuinely different units of work, per-product metrics collide. A customer buying pipeline monitoring, data-quality testing and lineage tracing from Nishkarsh would face three meters, three allowances and three overage rates, and the resulting invoice becomes an object of suspicion rather than a statement of value. The mature response, arrived at independently by most large infrastructure vendors, is an abstract internal currency — credits, units, tokens, consumption dollars — into which every product's work is converted at a published rate. This solves the invoice problem and creates two new ones. First, the credit becomes the value metric in the customer's mind, and the conversion rates become the real pricing decision, made quietly by a pricing committee rather than loudly in a launch. Second, credits decouple what the customer buys from what they consume, which introduces breakage: unused credits that expire. Breakage is profitable and corrosive in exactly the same proportion, and companies that come to depend on it have replaced a value metric with a float.

Two-sided markets: which side carries the meter

Nimantran Commerce, a Gurugram marketplace matching event organisers with venues and service providers, spent 2024 charging suppliers a subscription for listing access and 2025 arguing about whether to move to a take rate on booking value. The theoretical answer — meter the side with the higher willingness to pay and lower elasticity, subsidise the other — is correct and nearly useless, because it does not say what happens to the metric when the subsidised side's participation is what creates the value being metered. Nimantran's specific difficulty was disintermediation: a take rate on booking value creates an incentive for both sides to close the transaction off-platform, which means the metric must be defended by making on-platform settlement more convenient than the fee is painful. The general principle is that in two-sided markets the value metric and the platform's control of the transaction are the same problem; a metric denominated in transaction value is only collectable to the extent the platform is inside the transaction. Marketplaces that lose the payment rail lose the metric, usually within four quarters.

Regulated markets, where the metric can be legislated away

India offers the clearest live example anywhere of a value metric removed by policy. Merchant discount rate on UPI person-to-merchant transactions was set to zero by the government from January 2020, which eliminated at a stroke the per-transaction take rate that would have been the natural value metric for every payments participant in the stack. Firms that had built their monetisation on a percentage of transaction value had to reconstruct it elsewhere: in float, in lending distribution, in merchant software subscriptions, in settlement-cycle products. The lesson generalises beyond payments. Where a regulator has an interest in the affordability of the unit — the RBI in transactions, the IRDAI in insurance distribution commissions, TRAI in telecommunications tariffs, state health authorities in per-procedure pricing — a value metric denominated in that unit carries policy risk that belongs in the pricing decision itself, not in a risk register nobody reads. The practical expert habit is to ask, of any transaction-denominated metric, who other than the buyer has standing to object to it.

Hardware plus software

Niketan Devices manufactures smart water meters and sells them to municipal corporations and large residential estates, bundled with a consumption-analytics and leak-detection platform. The hardware has a bill of materials of ₹3,840 and an installed life of eight to ten years. The software's value scales with the number of connections monitored and, more meaningfully, with the volume of non-revenue water the platform helps recover. Three structural complications appear that pure-software teams do not face. The metric must survive the device's life, because a municipality will not renegotiate a metric tied to an asset it has capitalised. The metric must be denominated in something that continues to exist if the vendor's software is switched off, which pushes toward connections rather than analytics events. And the cash-flow shape of the hardware — large outlay at installation — pulls toward an upfront fee that structurally suppresses β. Firms in this position typically arrive at a split metric: a per-connection recurring fee that pays for the platform, plus a gain-share on recovered water that is aligned but capped. The gain-share is where the interesting failures live, because measuring the counterfactual volume of water that would have been lost requires a baseline both parties trust, and baselines are negotiated, not observed.

AI-native products, where the unit of work has no name

The hardest contemporary case is Aditya's. When software did what a person told it to do, seats were a defensible proxy for work because work required a person. An agent that operates continuously breaks the proxy in both directions: it does far more work than the seats suggest, and the amount of work is set by the customer's environment rather than by the customer's decisions. Three families of answer are in play across the industry. Per-consumption metrics — tokens, calls, credits — are perfectly cost-coupled and almost perfectly illegible to a buyer, who cannot forecast a token bill and will not try. Per-work-item metrics — resolutions, documents, obligations, tickets closed — are the current centre of gravity, with several customer-support vendors publicly pricing per automated resolution, because a work item is a unit the buyer already counts and can compare against the labour cost it displaces. Per-outcome metrics are the theoretically ideal and practically fragile answer, for the reason Table 2 records: outcomes are counterfactual, and counterfactuals are unauditable.

There is a second-order effect specific to AI products that deserves separate statement. Inference cost per unit of work has been falling fast and unevenly. A metric that is tightly cost-coupled therefore embeds a deflating cost base into a contract with a fixed price, which means a vendor who prices at a target margin today will be earning a substantially higher margin in eighteen months on the same unit — and will face a customer who reads the model-provider price announcements and expects to be passed the saving. Vendors who anticipate this write explicit price-review clauses tied to a published cost index; vendors who do not will be renegotiating from a defensive position, having captured a windfall they cannot justify in a room.

The organisational seams

Value metrics fail at organisational boundaries more often than at analytical ones, and four seams account for most of it.

The first is sales compensation. A consumption metric means bookings and revenue diverge, and a commission plan that pays on bookings will quietly reward representatives for selling large committed allowances that customers do not consume — which looks like excellent expansion for four quarters and appears as a wall of unconsumed commitment at the first renewal cycle. The second is revenue recognition. Under Ind AS 115 and its international equivalent, usage-based fees are variable consideration recognised as consumed, so a metric change moves revenue out of the predictable rateable bucket and into a bucket that depends on customer behaviour, which is Meera Vaidyanathan's objection and is not a finance department being obstructive. The third is the metering platform itself, usually owned by an infrastructure team with no commercial incentive and no service-level obligation to billing; when metering drifts, the failure surfaces as customer disputes weeks later, and the team that caused it never sees the cost. The fourth is support, where billing queries land. A metric's true cost includes the queue it creates, and that queue is invisible in every pricing model this author has seen presented to a board.

What mature companies actually do, as distinct from what they say, is instructive on all four points. They say they chose the metric that best tracks value. What they did was run the new metric in shadow mode alongside the old one for two to four quarters, publish a customer-facing meter so that the buyer could see the number accruing in real time, grandfather the largest accounts for a full contract cycle, rewrite the commission plan before announcing the metric rather than after, and accept a deliberate revenue reduction in the first year in exchange for a structurally growing base. The shadow period is the step most often skipped and the one whose absence is most reliably fatal.

6. Nine distinctions that separate the expert from the competent

The metric is a contract term before it is an analytical choice, and contracts have inertia the analysis does not. A metric written into a three-year master agreement with a most-favoured-nation clause and an annual uplift cap is not a variable a product manager can change; it is a liability with a maturity date. The tell that someone has internalised this is that they ask to see the standard contract template before they ask to see the usage data, and that their migration plan is organised by renewal date rather than by customer segment. The obvious reading — that the analysis determines the metric and the contract merely records it — is backwards in any company past about ₹100 crore of recurring revenue, where the achievable pace of change is set by the renewal calendar and nothing else.

A metric's correlation with value is a property of a moment, not of the metric. Nishkarsh's table count was a genuinely good metric in 2019, when tables were narrow, numerous and proportional to the data estate. It became a bad metric because customers' architecture changed, not because the original analysis was wrong. Experts therefore ask of any candidate metric not "does this track value" but "what technical or organisational change on the customer's side would break the correlation, and how likely is it within the contract term". The tell is a practitioner who names the specific technology shift that would kill their metric; the obvious reading — that a metric validated on eighteen months of data is validated — mistakes a backward-looking correlation for a forward-looking one.

The distribution matters more than the mean, and the mean is what gets presented. Almost every pricing deck shows the average customer's bill before and after. Almost every problem lives in the tails: the bottom quintile whose bill falls below the cost to serve them, and the top two or three accounts whose bill rises enough to trigger a procurement escalation that the model did not contemplate. The tell of an expert is that their first slide is a distribution with the tails annotated by name, and that they have already spoken to the three accounts at the top. The obvious reading is that a revenue-neutral migration is a safe migration; in fact a revenue-neutral migration with high dispersion is a migration in which a quarter of the base is being materially repriced in each direction simultaneously.

The customer's ability to verify the meter is worth more than the meter's accuracy. A slightly imprecise number the buyer can reproduce from their own systems generates fewer disputes, faster payment and better renewals than a perfectly precise number only the vendor can compute. This is why the most successful consumption metrics are denominated in things the buyer independently counts — orders, policies, contracts, employees, transactions — rather than in vendor-internal quantities like compute-seconds or index operations. The tell is that the vendor ships a usage dashboard with an export before it ships the new pricing. The obvious reading is that verification is a trust-building nicety; in practice it is the primary determinant of days sales outstanding under consumption pricing.

A hybrid metric is not a compromise but a portfolio, and should be reasoned about as one. When a company charges a platform fee plus consumption, it holds two revenue streams with different risk profiles: one uncorrelated with customer behaviour, one strongly correlated. The right question is not "what proportion feels balanced" but "what proportion of revenue do we need to be insensitive to customer usage in order to survive a demand shock". Companies that went into the 2022–23 software downturn with eighty percent consumption revenue discovered the answer the hard way. The tell of expertise is a stated target for the fixed share of revenue, justified by a downside scenario; the obvious reading — that more alignment is always better — ignores that alignment is symmetric and works in both directions.

The metric determines who inside the customer is your buyer, which determines the deal size you can ever reach. A seat metric makes the departmental manager the buyer, because seats are a headcount decision within their control. A consumption metric denominated in a business-level quantity makes the business owner the buyer, because the bill scales with their operations. This is a strategic choice disguised as a pricing choice: it sets the ceiling on deal size and the length of the sales cycle simultaneously. The tell is a practitioner who can name the title that signs under each candidate metric. The obvious reading treats the buyer as fixed and the metric as the variable; the causality runs at least as strongly the other way.

Metric changes leak information about the vendor's cost structure, and sophisticated buyers read it. When a vendor moves from seats to consumption shortly after launching an AI feature, a competent procurement team infers, correctly, that the feature has a marginal cost the vendor is trying to recover, and adjusts its negotiating position accordingly — frequently by demanding a cap, a fixed-price option, or visibility into the cost basis. The tell of an expert is that the migration narrative is prepared for this inference rather than surprised by it, and usually leads with it. The obvious reading is that pricing changes can be framed purely as customer benefit; buyers with pricing analysts on staff have stopped believing that framing.

Every metric has a gaming equilibrium, and the interesting question is what the equilibrium behaviour costs the customer. Metrics are not gameable or ungameable; they are gameable at some price. A per-message metric is gamed by batching, at the cost of latency. A per-seat metric is gamed by credential sharing, at the cost of audit exposure. A per-obligation metric would be gamed by narrowing the tracked estate, at the cost of the very coverage the product is bought for. The expert's move is to choose the metric whose gaming behaviour is most expensive to the customer in their own currency, which makes the metric self-enforcing without contractual policing. The tell is a practitioner who describes the gaming path and then explains why the customer will not take it. The obvious reading — that gaming should be prevented by contract terms — produces audit clauses, which produce adversarial relationships, which produce churn.

The decision to change a metric and the decision to change price levels must be made together and communicated separately. Made together, because a metric migration reveals the true dispersion of value across the base and almost always shows that the old price level was wrong for most of it; communicated separately, because a customer who perceives a metric change as a price increase will evaluate it as one, and the analytical case for the metric will never be heard. The tell is a migration in which the first wave is explicitly revenue-neutral per account, with price-level adjustments deferred to the following renewal. The obvious reading — that one might as well fix everything at once, since the contract is open anyway — is efficient and reliably destroys the goodwill the migration needs.

7. How this differs across product types and company stages

Some of the differences by product type are real and some are folklore, and it is worth separating them.

In consumer products the difference is real and it is about cognition, not economics. Consumers exhibit a well-documented flat-rate bias: they systematically choose flat tariffs over metered ones even when the metered tariff would have cost them less, because a predictable bill has option value against the anxiety of monitoring. The implication is not that consumer products have no value metric but that the metric operates behind a flat price, expressed as a tier boundary rather than as a per-unit rate — storage tiers, device counts, download allowances. A consumer product that meters visibly at the moment of use suppresses the very engagement it depends on, which is why per-minute mobile pricing in India collapsed into unlimited bundles within four years of data becoming cheap.

In business-to-business software sold to mid-market buyers the folklore is that consumption pricing is superior; the reality is that consumption pricing has a minimum viable operational sophistication on both sides. A mid-market buyer without a procurement function, a finance business partner and an internal cost-allocation model cannot manage a variable bill, and will experience it as a series of unpleasant surprises. Vendors selling into this segment who move to consumption without also shipping spend controls, alerts and hard caps are transferring an operational burden their customer cannot carry.

In enterprise the difference is real and it is about the budget cycle. Large Indian enterprises and global capability centres set annual technology budgets with limited in-year flexibility, which means a variable bill is not a pricing preference but a governance problem: an overrun must be explained to a committee that meets quarterly. The practical accommodation is the committed-consumption contract — the customer commits to a rupee amount for the year and draws it down against the metric — which converts a variable bill into a fixed budget line while preserving alignment at the margin, and which is now the dominant structure in enterprise infrastructure for exactly this reason.

In platforms and marketplaces the difference is real and was covered above: the metric is only as collectable as the platform's position in the transaction. In hardware and physical goods the difference is real and concerns the asset's life and the buyer's capitalisation treatment, also covered above. In AI-native products the difference is real and concerns the reappearance of marginal cost. Where the difference is largely folklore is in the distinction between developer tools and other B2B software: developer products are often held to require consumption pricing because developers "expect" it, but the operative fact is not developer preference, it is that developer products are usually infrastructure with a genuine marginal cost and a self-serve motion that cannot support negotiation. A developer tool with zero marginal cost sold through a sales team behaves like any other enterprise product.

Stage changes the calculus in a way that is often stated as a platitude and is worth making precise. The binding constraint at seed stage is not metric quality but evidence: a company with nine customers cannot estimate β, cannot observe dispersion, and cannot know which technical shift will break the correlation, so the correct behaviour is to choose the simplest metric the buyer already counts and to instrument everything else without billing it. The binding constraint at growth stage is the renewal calendar and the commission plan. The binding constraint at scale is the installed base's contracts and the reported-metrics narrative that public or late-stage investors have been given; a company that has spent three years telling the market its net revenue retention is 118 percent cannot casually adopt a metric that will make that number volatile, however correct the metric is. This is a real constraint, not a failure of nerve, and pretending otherwise is how product leaders lose credibility with their own finance function.

8. Three worked examples

Example one: Nishkarsh Systems — recovering the level after resetting the metric

Sharanya's team modelled the migration across the full base rather than on representative accounts, and the distribution is the point. Under the proposed three-part tariff, 61 accounts saw a bill increase above ten percent, 94 saw a change within ten percent either way, and 59 saw a decrease above ten percent. Total first-year revenue was ₹171 crore against ₹186 crore, a deliberate eight percent reset. The modelled second year, holding customer growth at the observed 26 percent and applying the tariff mechanically, was ₹208 crore. The crossing point was month nineteen.

Example two: Nimantran Commerce — the metric that had to be defended, not just chosen

Nimantran moved from a ₹24,000 annual supplier subscription to a 4.5 percent take rate on booking value in April 2025, across 3,100 active suppliers. Gross booking value in the trailing year had been ₹412 crore, implying ₹18.5 crore of take-rate revenue against ₹7.4 crore of subscription revenue. The realised figure for the first twelve months was ₹11.2 crore. The gap was not price resistance; it was leakage. Suppliers used Nimantran to find the customer and settled directly for roughly thirty-eight percent of the value they sourced through the platform. Nimantran's response was not enforcement but product: escrowed payments with release on event completion, which suppliers wanted because event clients in India routinely delay final payments, and a dispute-resolution service available only on platform-settled bookings. On-platform settlement rose from 62 to 84 percent over the following three quarters. The general lesson is that a transaction-denominated value metric is a claim on a transaction the platform must continuously earn the right to sit inside, and the budget for earning that right belongs in the pricing business case.

Example three: Nilambari Health Cloud — a correct metric that failed anyway

Nilambari sold a hospital information system to mid-sized private hospitals across Maharashtra, Gujarat and Telangana, priced at ₹1,450 per sanctioned bed per month across 31 hospital groups. In 2023 its leadership concluded, on entirely sound reasoning, that beds were a poor proxy: occupancy varied from 41 to 94 percent, the software's work was driven by patient episodes rather than by beds, and the most valuable customers were the busiest rather than the largest. They moved to ₹78 per completed episode of care.

The analysis was right and the migration was a disaster. Three things went wrong, and only the third was foreseeable in hindsight only.

First, the episode count lived in the hospital's own admission-discharge-transfer workflow, which Nilambari's system recorded but did not control. Hospitals used the module inconsistently — day-care procedures were sometimes recorded as episodes and sometimes not, and a single patient transferred between departments could generate one episode or three depending on how the front desk was trained. The vendor's number and the customer's number disagreed, systematically, by between four and nineteen percent.

Second, the disagreement arrived monthly, on an invoice, to a hospital finance office that had no way to audit it. Days sales outstanding across the base rose from 46 to 118. Credit notes in FY24 totalled ₹1.9 crore against ₹21 crore of billings. Nine of the 31 groups disputed at least one invoice; four escalated to their boards; three declined to renew.

Third, and most damaging, the metric aligned Nilambari's revenue with hospital throughput at a moment when several of its customers were under scrutiny over admission practices. A vendor whose revenue rises with the number of admissions is in an uncomfortable position when a payer or a regulator asks who benefits from an admission. Nobody alleged anything improper; the mere structural appearance of the incentive was enough to make two hospital groups' compliance officers object to the contract independently of its cost.

9. Failure modes, their early warnings and the cost of late detection

Silent decay. The metric was right and the world moved. The early warning is a widening gap between growth in the billed metric and growth in any operational metric the company tracks — at Nishkarsh, four percent against thirty-one percent, visible for at least six quarters before anyone drew the chart. The diagnostic question is: over the last eight quarters, which of our operational counters grew fastest, and why is it not the one on the invoice? Caught early, decay is a repricing at the next renewal. Caught late, it is a repricing conducted from a position of weakness against a customer who has already discovered the arbitrage, as the Mumbai insurer had.

The unmetered meter. The metric was adopted before the instrumentation was trustworthy. The early warning is not disputes — disputes are the late warning — but a rising proportion of invoices requiring manual adjustment before issue, a number that lives in a finance operations spreadsheet and is almost never reported upward. The diagnostic question is: what percentage of last month's invoices was issued exactly as the billing system computed it? Caught early, this costs an engineering quarter. Caught late, it costs days sales outstanding, credit notes and, as at Nilambari, renewals.

Margin inversion. The metric is uncoupled from a cost that has become material. The early warning is variance in gross margin by account rather than a fall in average gross margin; the average can look healthy while the largest accounts are deeply negative. The diagnostic question is: what is our contribution margin for the tenth-percentile account by margin, not the mean? Caught early, it is a packaging change. Caught late, it is Nitara's position in January 2026, in which the company's commercial success and its solvency were pointing in opposite directions.

Commission-plan veto. The metric changed and the compensation plan did not. The early warning is a sudden increase in the size of committed allowances sold relative to trailing consumption — representatives optimising for the booking they are paid on. The diagnostic question is: what proportion of committed consumption sold in the last two quarters has actually been consumed? Caught early, it is a plan amendment. Caught late, it is a cohort of renewals in which customers are asked to re-commit to a level they demonstrably did not need, which is the single most reliable generator of contraction in consumption businesses.

Metric proliferation. Each new product arrived with its own unit and nobody consolidated. The early warning is the length of the invoice and the emergence of an internal "pricing exceptions" list with more than a handful of entries. The diagnostic question is: how many distinct units appear on the invoice of our median multi-product customer? Caught early, it is a credit currency designed deliberately. Caught late, it is a credit currency designed under duress, with conversion rates set to reproduce existing revenue rather than to express relative value, which locks the mispricing in for years.

The incentive that reads badly. The metric aligns vendor revenue with a customer behaviour that a third party — a regulator, a payer, a journalist, an internal compliance officer — has reason to scrutinise. The early warning is an objection from someone on the customer's side who is not the buyer. The diagnostic question is: if our revenue rises, whose behaviour must have increased, and would that person be comfortable explaining it? Caught early, it is a metric substitution. Caught late, it is Nilambari's third problem, which cost the relationship rather than the invoice.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Four disputes in this area are live, and are not resolved by any evidence currently available. Each is stated here in the strongest form its proponents would recognise.

Whether alignment or legibility should dominate when they conflict. The alignment position holds that a bill which moves with value is self-justifying, converts customer success into vendor revenue without a sales motion, and is the only structure that survives a long relationship; its evidence is the durable outperformance of consumption-priced infrastructure businesses on net revenue retention and the repeated pattern of seat-based vendors being disrupted from below. The legibility position holds that this evidence is confounded by market growth, that buyers demonstrably pay a premium for predictable bills, and that the same consumption-priced businesses showed far worse revenue volatility when demand turned; its evidence is the flat-rate bias literature and the 2022–23 experience. What would have to be true for the alignment position to be wrong: that the premium buyers pay for predictability exceeds the expansion that alignment generates, over a full cycle rather than a growth phase. Nobody has measured this cleanly, because the two structures are not randomly assigned.

Whether the metric should track value or willingness to pay when these come apart. The screening position, which has the stronger formal foundation, holds that the purpose of a price schedule is to sort buyers, and that a metric correlated with willingness to pay will out-earn one correlated with value whenever the two diverge — which they do whenever a low-value use is made by a high-budget buyer. The alignment position holds that metrics which extract without delivering are detected and punished by buyers over multi-year relationships, and that the formal models assume a single-shot interaction that does not describe subscription software. What would have to be true for the screening position to be wrong: that reputational and renewal effects are large enough to outweigh the extraction gain, which depends on how transparent the market is and how switchable the product is — both of which vary enormously by category, which may be why the dispute persists.

Whether AI products should be priced on work done or on outcomes achieved. The outcome position holds that outcome pricing is where the category is going because it is the only structure a buyer comparing software against labour can evaluate directly, and that measurement difficulties are engineering problems that will yield. The work-done position holds that outcomes are counterfactual, that any counterfactual can be disputed, that a vendor whose revenue falls as its product improves has a structural problem no measurement advance will fix, and that every historical attempt at outcome pricing outside a few narrow domains has collapsed back into input pricing. What would have to be true for the outcome position to be wrong: that no auditable baseline can be constructed for most outcomes, which is currently the empirical situation but is not obviously a permanent one.

Whether a company should ever change its value metric for its existing base, as opposed to only for new customers. The migration position holds that a base priced on a decayed metric is a slow leak that compounds, that grandfathering creates two products and two roadmaps, and that the disruption of migration is a one-time cost against a permanent gain. The grandfathering position holds that the realised cost of migrations is consistently underestimated — support load, churn, sales distraction, the goodwill spent — that most of the arithmetic gain can be captured by pricing new customers correctly and letting the old base run off naturally, and that companies that migrate their base are frequently solving a narrative problem for investors rather than an economic problem for themselves. What would have to be true for the migration position to be wrong: that base run-off is fast enough that the mispriced cohort becomes immaterial before the leak does real damage, which depends on churn rates the migration advocates are usually trying to reduce.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this topic can name the tests a metric should pass and can point at a seat-based product and say it should probably be usage-based. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four observable ways.

They start from the contract and the calendar, not from the data. Their first question in any metric conversation is which accounts renew when, what the notice periods are, and what the uplift caps say, because those facts bound the achievable answer and the data does not.

They compute the distribution before the mean, and they can name the accounts in both tails. They arrive at the pricing review with a list of five customers they have already spoken to, and their proposal already contains the accommodation each of those five will need. This is the single most reliable behavioural marker, because it cannot be faked by analysis alone.

They treat the meter as part of the product. The customer-facing usage view, the export, the alerting, the dispute window and the reconciliation procedure appear in the roadmap as features with owners and dates, ahead of the pricing announcement rather than behind it. They will delay a metric change by a quarter to ship the meter first, and they can explain why in terms of days sales outstanding rather than in terms of trust.

And they hold the disagreements in section ten as genuinely open, which shows up as a willingness to choose differently in different parts of the same portfolio — consumption for the infrastructure product sold to engineers, a committed-consumption contract for the enterprise suite, a flat tier for the self-serve tool — rather than as a house doctrine applied uniformly. A practitioner who believes there is one right answer to this topic has not yet met a case where their answer was wrong.

12. What Sharanya and Aditya decided

Sharanya Iyer took a three-part tariff to Nishkarsh's board on 3 March 2026, with four qualifications she considered non-negotiable. The metric would be billions of rows scanned, not tables and not incidents — incidents had tested better on alignment but failed claim four decisively, because a customer could reduce incidents by reducing coverage, which would have made Nishkarsh's revenue fall as its customers' data quality improved. The migration would run by renewal date over seven quarters, with the twelve largest accounts grandfathered for a full cycle and approached individually. The first wave would be explicitly revenue-neutral per account, with the platform fee tuned per customer to reproduce the existing bill at current usage, so that the metric change and any price change were separated in time. And the customer-facing meter, with export and a 72-hour dispute window, would ship two quarters before the first migrated invoice. She accepted Meera's revenue-recognition consequence and asked her to brief the prospective investors on it before the model changed rather than after. For the Mumbai insurer she proposed a two-year agreement at ₹2.9 crore a year — below the expiring ₹4.1 crore, above the ₹87 lakh the old schedule would have produced — and told Kabir Sethi to present it as what it was, a reset in exchange for a structure that would not punish the insurer for good engineering again.

Aditya Shenoy chose differently, and the difference is the point of putting the two cases side by side. Nitara adopted obligations under management as the primary metric, at ₹9 per obligation per month with a tiered floor, but did not adopt it alone. Because a general counsel cannot state their obligation count before signing, Nitara made the first ninety days a fixed-fee discovery engagement priced at ₹6 lakh, at the end of which the obligation count was established, jointly reviewed, and became the contract baseline — converting an unknowable number into a known one before the buyer had to commit to it. Inference cost was addressed separately, by a clause tying the per-obligation rate to an annual review against Nitara's published cost basis, with any reduction of more than twenty percent passed through at fifty percent. Shenoy declined breaches averted entirely, despite two board members preferring it, on the grounds that he was not willing to run a company whose revenue fell as its product improved. For the Chennai conglomerate the new structure implied a bill of ₹27.9 lakh a month against ₹2.88 lakh, and Shenoy's judgement — contested inside his own company — was that a client paying nine seats for a system tracking 310,000 obligations had a bill so far below the value received that the conversation was winnable, provided it began with the obligation ledger rather than with the price.

Questions for discussion

  1. Nishkarsh's first migration wave is revenue-neutral per account by construction, which means the company absorbs a year of foregone price correction in exchange for a cleaner narrative. Nitara, facing a far worse economic position, proposes a nearly tenfold increase for its largest client in a single step. Under what conditions is each the right sequencing decision, and what does the difference reveal about how urgency should change pricing tactics?
  2. Sharanya rejected "incidents detected" despite it scoring higher on pass-through than rows scanned, because a customer could reduce it by reducing coverage. Aditya rejected "breaches averted" on closely related grounds. Yet several AI vendors are building businesses on precisely such outcome metrics. What would have to be true about a market for an outcome metric with an inverse cost correlation to be the right choice?
  3. Meera Vaidyanathan's objection was about revenue recognition and reported net revenue retention, not about customer value. Is a finance constraint of this kind a legitimate input to the choice of value metric, or a distortion that a product leader should argue against? What is the strongest version of the opposing case to the one you hold?

13. Going deeper

Revenue models
The value metric is the argument of the pricing function; the revenue model is the function's shape and who pays it. Reading them together clarifies which problems are metric problems and which are model problems — a distinction that decides whether a fix is a repricing or a restructuring.
North Star metric
The strongest test of a value metric is whether it is the same quantity the company already organises around. Where the two diverge, one of them is wrong, and working out which is a more revealing exercise than either alone.
Monetisation as a growth lever
Pass-through determines how much of a company's growth arrives without a sales motion. This topic quantifies that lever and sets it against acquisition and retention, which is the comparison a general manager actually has to make when allocating a year.
Packaging: good / better / best
Once the unit is chosen, tiering decides how much of it each segment gets and at what rate. Packaging is where the screening school does most of its work, and where a single metric is made to serve buyers with very different willingness to pay.
Value-based, cost-plus and competitive pricing
This page deliberately left the price level alone. That topic returns to it, and its treatment of cost-plus is now more relevant than it was for twenty years, because AI has made marginal cost material again.
Pricing APIs and developer products
The clearest laboratory for consumption metrics, because the buyer is technical, the metering is native and the alternatives are visible. It also shows the limits: developer-facing metrics that are perfectly cost-coupled are frequently unforecastable, and the resulting spend-control features are as important as the price.
Changing the value metric
The direct sequel. Everything in section nine about migration sequencing, grandfathering, commission plans and shadow periods is treated there as the primary subject rather than as a consequence.
When to charge
The timing question sits underneath the metric question: a metric that accrues continuously and a bill that arrives annually are a working-capital decision as much as a pricing one, and one that Nilambari's episode ledger was in part designed to solve.
Willingness-to-pay research
The empirical instrument for the screening school's claims. Conjoint and Van Westendorp studies are usually run on price levels; running them on metric choice — asking buyers to trade off units rather than amounts — is less common and considerably more informative.
Freemium vs free trial
The free tier is a statement about the metric: where the allowance boundary sits determines who converts and on what evidence. A free tier bounded by the wrong unit will admit the wrong users and teach the wrong lesson about conversion.
What pricing signals
The metric communicates what a company believes it is selling, often more loudly than its positioning does. Section six's point about buyers inferring cost structure from metric changes belongs to this topic as much as to this one.
AI cost-to-serve and pricing
The quantitative treatment of the cost-coupling school. Nitara's entire situation is an instance of it, and the deflation problem — falling inference costs inside fixed-price contracts — is handled there in detail.
Discounting and promotions
Discounts are modifications to the pricing function that frequently destroy the metric's alignment without anyone noticing: a heavily discounted overage rate converts a consumption contract back into a flat fee in economic substance while leaving it a consumption contract on paper.

The Value Metric

Per what unit should we charge, so that price rises and falls with the value the customer actually receives?

1. A festive quarter that should have been a celebration

On the second Monday of October 2024, Ananya Krishnan opened the board deck for Karigar Cloud with a chart she had built three times and deleted twice. Karigar Cloud sold an order-orchestration platform to direct-to-consumer brands in India — the software that sat between a brand's storefront and its courier partners, deciding which warehouse should ship an order, which courier should carry it, and, since the previous spring, whether a given order looked fraudulent before it left the warehouse. Ananya was the company's vice-president of product, and the chart she kept redrawing showed two lines that were not supposed to diverge the way they had. The first line was Karigar's monthly recurring revenue, which had grown at a tidy, unremarkable 4–6 percent a month all year. The second line was the number of shipments the platform had processed for its customers, which had roughly tripled in the six weeks since the festive season began, as apparel and electronics brands pushed inventory through Diwali sales.

The mismatch mattered because Karigar was eleven weeks from closing a Series C round, and the lead investor's associate had asked, in the diligence call the previous Thursday, a question Ananya could not answer cleanly: "Your biggest customers are shipping three times the volume this quarter. Why isn't that showing up in revenue?" The honest answer was that Karigar charged per seat — ₹8,000 per named user per month — and none of its customers had needed to add a single user to process three times as many orders. A ten-person operations team at a mid-sized apparel brand like Kanika Fashions could push 30,000 shipments through the platform in a slow month and 90,000 in a festive month using the exact same ten logins. The software was doing dramatically more work, absorbing dramatically more compute for its new AI-based fraud-screening feature, which scored every order for return risk before dispatch — and Karigar was being paid exactly the same amount either way. Ananya's problem was not a sales problem or a retention problem. It was that Karigar had chosen the wrong unit to charge for, four years earlier, when the choice had felt too small to deliberate over. She had, without quite naming it that way, inherited the wrong value metric, and now she had eleven weeks to fix it before it became a line item in a term sheet.

2. The idea: charge for the unit that moves with value

A value metric is the unit a company attaches its price to — the thing that, when it goes up, the customer's bill goes up too, and when it goes up, the customer should also feel they got more. Salesforce's value metric is the seat. Twilio's is the message or the minute. Snowflake's is the compute-second. Zomato's, on its restaurant-facing side, is a percentage of the order value it routes. In every one of these cases the company is not merely deciding how much to charge; it is deciding for what, and that second decision is prior to the first, because it sets the shape of the relationship between the customer's success and the vendor's revenue for the life of the account.

The idea has a lineage worth knowing precisely because Ananya's board would expect her to know it. Value-based pricing as a discipline was formalised by the marketing scholar Thomas Nagle, whose 1987 book The Strategy and Tactics of Pricing argued that price should be set from the customer's perceived value backward, not from cost forward. But "value metric" as a specific, named decision — distinct from the price level itself — entered product and pricing practice later, through the software industry's shift to recurring revenue in the 2010s. Consultants and operators such as Patrick Campbell at ProfitWell and Kyle Poyar at OpenView Partners popularised the term as SaaS companies discovered that flat, seat-based licensing was leaving money on the table for products whose value scaled with usage rather than headcount, and was in some cases actively punishing customers who succeeded. The problem the concept was invented to solve is this: a company can set an excellent price and still destroy the relationship between price and value if it attaches that price to the wrong thing.

The sentence Ananya could say in the boardroom without sounding glib: "We should charge for the thing that grows when our customer's business grows — not for the thing that happens to be easiest for us to bill."

It is worth being precise about what the value metric is not. It is not the price itself — ₹0.50 per shipment and ₹5 per shipment are two prices on the same value metric. It is not a usage metric in the generic sense either, because plenty of things a customer uses do not track the value they receive; logins, page views and support tickets are all usage, but charging for any of them would tie revenue to something closer to friction than to benefit. The value metric is specifically the unit that a rational, informed customer would look at and say: yes, when this number is larger, I am plainly getting more from the product.

3. How the choice actually gets made

Choosing a value metric is not a single insight; it is a short sequence of tests, and Ananya's team skipped most of them the first time round because Karigar, in 2020, had exactly one customer, no usage data, and an urgent need to send an invoice. Doing it properly, four years later, meant working through the sequence deliberately.

The first test is identifying the value driver: the thing that, in the customer's own account of their business, gets better because of the product. For Karigar, that was not "logins" or "warehouses connected." It was shipments successfully routed and screened — the unit in which a brand's operations head measured their own throughput. The second test is correlation: does the candidate metric rise and fall with the customer's own success, across many customers, not just the one in front of you? Ananya's team pulled eighteen months of data and found that shipment volume correlated with a customer's own revenue at 0.86 across their base of forty-one accounts, while seat count correlated at 0.31 — seats were sticky and slow-moving regardless of how a brand's season was going, which was precisely the disconnect the board had noticed.

The third test, meterability, is the one engineers usually raise first and product managers usually raise too late: can you actually instrument the unit cleanly, at low cost, in a way both sides trust? Karigar already logged every shipment for operational reasons, so metering was nearly free; a company charging by "value delivered" in some softer sense would fail this test immediately, because a unit nobody can count cleanly cannot anchor an invoice. The fourth test, predictability, protects the buyer: a finance team approving a vendor contract needs to forecast next quarter's spend within a reasonable band, so a metric that swings unpredictably, however well it tracks value, creates budget anxiety that shows up later as churn. The fifth test, gameability, protects the seller: if customers can shrink the metric without shrinking the value they receive — splitting one large shipment into several small ones to reduce a per-shipment count, for instance — the metric will erode under its own popularity. A workable value metric survives all five; Karigar's seat-based metric had only ever cleared the third and fourth.

4. The arithmetic, worked twice

Ananya modelled the switch using two representative customers from Karigar's base: Kanika Fashions, a mid-sized apparel brand with ten operations seats, and a much larger customer, the electronics retailer that ran roughly four times Kanika's shipment volume through the platform. Under the old model, both paid strictly for seats.
