Read the seat column first: Kanika's bill is flat at ₹48,000 whether the platform processes 30,000 or 90,000 shipments, because nothing about a festive surge required a new login. Now read the usage columns: in a normal month, Kanika's usage-based bill of ₹16,500 is actually lower than the seat-based bill, which looks at first like a revenue loss — and this is exactly the number that made Karigar's finance lead nervous when Ananya first presented it. But look at the festive column: the same customer, doing three times its normal volume, now pays ₹49,500, almost exactly what the flat seat price used to charge in every month regardless of volume, and the electronics retailer's bill nearly triples, from ₹66,000 to ₹1,98,000, tracking a surge in shipments that under the old model would have generated zero additional revenue. The platform floor of ₹15,000 does the second piece of work: it guarantees Karigar a predictable minimum even from a quiet customer in a quiet month, so the switch is not simply "usage instead of seats" but "a floor for predictability, plus usage for alignment."

Now change one input and watch the answer move. Suppose the AI fraud-screening feature, which scores every shipment against a return-risk model, costs Karigar itself ₹0.09 per shipment scored in inference compute — a real, variable cost of goods that seat-based pricing had been quietly absorbing out of gross margin. If Karigar prices the base platform at ₹0.55 per shipment but bundles fraud-screening in for free, its gross margin on the electronics retailer's festive month falls from roughly 84 percent to just under 68 percent, because 360,000 shipments at ₹0.09 is ₹32,400 of compute cost eaten by a bill that did not change. Price the fraud-screening separately, at ₹0.15 per shipment scored, with a floor of ₹0.09 above cost, and the picture changes again: the same festive month now brings in an additional ₹54,000 specifically for the AI feature, comfortably covering its own inference bill and leaving a margin buffer. The arithmetic shows something the first pass could not: the value metric decision and the cost-to-serve decision are not two separate conversations once a product has an AI layer with a real marginal cost per action. They have to be solved together, unit by unit.

5. Eight distinctions a learner has to earn

Value metric, pricing metric and usage metric are three different words for three different things.

People use them interchangeably and it costs them clarity. The usage metric is anything the system happens to log. The pricing metric is whatever a company has, in practice, chosen to bill against, which may or may not track value at all — per-seat pricing for a product whose value scales with output is a pricing metric that has drifted away from being a value metric. The value metric, properly defined, is the pricing metric that has been deliberately chosen because it passes the five tests above. A team that says "our value metric is seats" without having tested that claim is usually describing a historical accident, not a decision.

Alignment and predictability pull in opposite directions, and the right answer is a compromise, not a winner.

The most value-aligned metric is often the least predictable one for the buyer, and a metric optimised purely for predictability, like a flat annual fee, is the least aligned with value of all. Karigar's platform floor is exactly this compromise made visible: pure usage pricing would have been more aligned but less forecastable, and Ananya chose to sacrifice a little of each rather than maximise either.

A value metric only earns its name where value genuinely scales with the unit; where it doesn't, the whole exercise misfires.

Some products deliver value in a step function rather than a slope — a compliance tool that prevents a single catastrophic fine delivers most of its value the moment it is switched on, not in proportion to how many documents it scans afterward. Forcing a per-document value metric onto that kind of product manufactures a false sense of rigor; the honest value metric there may simply be "protected," priced as a flat subscription, with usage metrics tracked for operational reasons but never billed.

It is routinely confused with the North Star metric, and the confusion is understandable because the two are meant to be close.

A company's North Star metric is the single number the whole organisation rallies around as the best proxy for value delivered at scale; the value metric is the unit inside the revenue model that a pricing team actually bills against. The best value metric tracks the North Star closely, but they are not required to be identical, and a company can have excellent clarity about its North Star while still billing on an unrelated, legacy unit — which is precisely the gap Ananya was closing.

The value metric tells you what to charge for, never how much.

Choosing "shipments processed" as Karigar's unit says nothing about whether the right number is ₹0.30 or ₹1.20 per shipment; that second question still requires a separate value-based pricing exercise — conjoint studies, willingness-to-pay interviews, competitive benchmarking — that a good value metric merely makes possible to run honestly. Teams that stop at "we found our value metric" and skip the pricing-level research have done half a job and will feel it at the next renewal cycle.

Gameability rarely shows up until the metric has already succeeded, which makes it dangerous.

Early in a rollout, no customer has the scale or the incentive to game a metric; the behaviour appears only once real money is at stake, often years later, at which point unwinding a metric that has become contractually entrenched is far more expensive than choosing carefully the first time. A thoughtful newcomer should ask, before shipping a new value metric: "if this customer's finance team spent an afternoon on it, how would they shrink this number without changing what they actually do?"

Metering cost is a real cost, not a footnote, and it changes which metrics are even eligible.

A value metric that requires expensive, brittle instrumentation to bill accurately — reconciling usage across three microservices with eventual consistency, for instance — can be correct in principle and still wrong in practice if the billing disputes it generates cost more in support time than the revenue precision is worth. This is why so many companies choose a value metric one level coarser than the truest driver of value: not "seconds of compute," which is precise but exhausting to reconcile, but "compute credits," a rounded, auditable proxy.

The value metric is not a permanent fixture; it is a decision with a shelf life tied to how the product itself changes.

The moment a company adds a genuinely new source of value — Karigar's AI fraud screening is the clean example — the existing value metric may quietly stop covering the whole of what customers now receive, and the honest response is either to extend the metric or add a second one, never to assume the old unit still captures everything. This is also why "changing the value metric" is treated as its own topic downstream of this one: it is a live, recurring decision, not a one-time ritual performed at founding.

6. How the same idea looks different by product type and by stage

In consumer products the value metric is frequently implicit rather than billed line by line: Spotify's value metric is arguably "hours of ad-free listening," but the price a subscriber sees is a flat monthly fee, because consumers resist metered billing for everyday habits even when a truer value-aligned unit exists underneath. Dropbox's storage-gigabyte is a rarer consumer example of an explicit, visible value metric, chosen because storage is a unit an ordinary user intuitively understands and can watch grow. In B2B software the value metric is usually explicit and often contested in the sales process itself: Salesforce's seat, Twilio's message, Snowflake's compute-second and HubSpot's contact count are all value metrics that a buyer's procurement team will interrogate line by line, which is exactly the scrutiny Ananya was facing from her own investors. In marketplaces the value metric collapses neatly onto a percentage of the transaction the platform enables — Zomato and Amazon both charge sellers a share of gross merchandise value, a metric that scales automatically with a seller's own success and needs almost no separate justification, because it is already denominated in the currency both sides care about.

Stage matters as much as product type. An early-stage company, as Karigar was in 2020, is usually right to choose the simplest defensible metric — even an imperfect one like seats — because the priority is minimising friction in the buying decision while the product and its usage patterns are still being discovered; a first-time buyer facing a complicated, multi-variable usage price alongside an unfamiliar vendor adds a second source of hesitation the deal cannot afford. A larger, data-rich company has both the obligation and the means to move toward a more sophisticated, often hybrid metric, precisely because it now has eighteen months of usage data across dozens of accounts to prove the new metric is fairer, not just more lucrative, and enough commercial leverage to manage the renegotiation without losing the relationship. Freshworks and Zoho, both Indian software companies operating at global scale, illustrate this arc publicly: their early flat per-agent pricing has, over successive years, grown extra usage-based and consumption-based layers alongside the seat, rather than replacing it outright, which is the pattern Ananya ultimately borrowed for Karigar rather than a clean rip-and-replace.

7. Where teams go wrong, and how to catch it cheaply

The first common mistake is billing on the unit that is easiest to sell rather than the unit that tracks value, and its symptom is exactly what Ananya saw: expansion revenue that stays flat while a customer's own usage visibly grows. The underlying misunderstanding is treating the value metric as a sales-enablement choice rather than an economic one. The cheapest diagnostic is the correlation check from Section 3: pull twelve to eighteen months of data and correlate revenue per account against usage growth per account; a coefficient meaningfully below 0.6 across a reasonable sample is a warning sign worth taking to the board before the board brings it to you.

The second mistake is choosing a metric that is well aligned but unpredictable for the buyer, and its symptom is pushback from procurement at renewal, or churn immediately following an unusually large invoice. The underlying misunderstanding is assuming alignment alone earns customer trust; in fact, a finance team that cannot forecast a vendor's bill within a reasonable band will often prefer a worse-aligned but predictable vendor. The cheapest diagnostic is simply to ask a handful of customer finance contacts, before rollout, to estimate their own bill for next quarter under the proposed metric, and see how wide their guesses are.

The third mistake, increasingly common wherever an AI feature has been added to an existing product, is pricing the new capability on the old value metric without checking its cost to serve, and its symptom is a gross margin that quietly erodes precisely among the heaviest, most engaged customers — the ones a company should be most pleased to see growing. The underlying misunderstanding is treating inference cost as an engineering concern rather than a pricing input. The cheapest diagnostic is a single spreadsheet column: cost-to-serve per unit of the value metric, sitting directly next to price-per-unit, recomputed every time a new AI capability ships.

The fourth mistake is treating the value metric as settled forever once chosen, and its symptom is a pricing model that steadily loses relevance to what the product actually does, discovered only when a customer or an investor asks an uncomfortable question in a room. The underlying misunderstanding is forgetting that the value metric is downstream of the product's North Star metric, and that a company's North Star is expected to evolve as the product matures. The cheapest diagnostic is a standing calendar reminder, once a year, to lay the current value metric next to the current North Star metric and ask, plainly, whether they still point at the same thing.

8. What good looks like

Twilio is the reference case product teams reach for precisely because its value metric — the message sent, the minute connected — was chosen at founding to be inseparable from the moment a developer's product actually worked, and has needed only extension, never replacement, as the company added voice, video and verification products each with their own cleanly metered unit. The discipline worth copying is not the specific unit but the standard: every new product line at Twilio has shipped alongside a metering decision made with the same rigor as the feature itself, not bolted on afterward by a finance team. At Karigar, doing this well meant Ananya's team ran the five-test framework on the fraud-screening feature before writing a line of billing code, priced it separately from the base platform with a margin floor pinned explicitly to inference cost, and piloted the combined model with six customers — including Kanika Fashions — for a full quarter before proposing it to the whole base, watching specifically for gaming behaviour and forecasting complaints rather than assuming the arithmetic alone had settled the question.

9. What Ananya decided, and what to read next

Ananya took two decisions to Karigar's board, not one. The primary value metric would move from seats to shipments processed, with a ₹15,000 monthly platform floor to preserve forecastability for smaller customers and protect Karigar's own revenue base in quiet months. The AI fraud-screening feature would be metered and priced separately, at ₹0.15 per shipment scored against a documented inference cost of ₹0.09, so that the feature's own economics would never again be invisible inside a flat fee. The reasoning she gave the board was the same reasoning this page has walked through: a value metric has to survive correlation, meterability, predictability and gameability tests together, and a company that adds a cost-bearing AI capability without re-running that test on its pricing is quietly funding that capability out of its own gross margin. The pilot with six accounts, including Kanika Fashions, would run one more quarter before the model reached the full base, precisely because Ananya had learned, the hard way, that a value metric is a hypothesis about customer behaviour and deserves to be tested like one before it is written into a term sheet.

From here, the two natural next readings are packaging — good, better and best — which asks how a single value metric gets split across tiers so different customers self-select the right amount of it; and value-based, cost-plus and competitive pricing, which returns to the question this page deliberately set aside: once the unit is chosen, what number should sit next to it. A reader who wants to test their own grasp of this page should sit with two questions before moving on. First, for a product they use or build themselves, what is the single unit that, if it doubled, would make the customer feel they had plainly received twice the value — and is that the unit currently being billed? Second, where in that same product does a cost that scales per unit, especially an AI inference cost, currently hide inside a price that does not scale at all?

Payodhi Water Infrastructure: What Is a Kilolitre Worth?

An ambiguous case on the value metric in a fifteen-year industrial water concession

1. Sunday night, Karur

At a quarter to eleven on Sunday, 1 November 2026, Poonam Lalwani was still at the long table on Kovai Road in Karur with three printouts in front of her, each stating how much effluent the Perundurai plant had treated in FY2025-26. The first said 9,41,700 kilolitres. The second said 8,77,825. The third said 9,89,880. None was a mistake.

Lalwani ran contracts and commercial at Payodhi Water Infrastructure Private Limited. At half past ten she would face the eighteen dyeing and bleaching units of the Ittefaq Dyers' Common Effluent Society, with their notice under Article 18.4 of the concession open in front of everybody. It asked Payodhi to reopen the basis on which it charged. Not the rate — the basis. Per what.

The rate was ₹ 148 per kilolitre of effluent received, which on the concession's basis produced an invoice of ₹ 1,393.72 lakh. The society had paid the first half, then begun paying on its members' own readings, withholding ₹ 47.27 lakh. The Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board wanted a metering protocol by 15 November, its own inspection having produced the third number — the largest, and never invoiced.

The spread between highest and lowest was ₹ 165.84 lakh. Perundurai's EBITDA was ₹ 320.00 lakh. More than half the plant's earnings turned not on work done but on whose meter you believed.

2. How Payodhi got here

Gopal Vaswani founded Payodhi in Karur in 2014, maintaining textile mills' in-house effluent plants. Its first build-own-operate plant came in 2017 at Namakkal, per kilolitre received; a second at Dindigul in 2018, for a sago and starch cluster whose discharge was too seasonal to meter, so Payodhi took a fixed monthly availability charge instead (Exhibit 1). Nobody has since asked whether that contract works.

Perundurai was the leap: a fifteen-year concession, won in February 2019, for a 3,000 kilolitre-a-day plant with zero liquid discharge. To win it Payodhi conceded three things — a tariff frozen at ₹ 132 per kilolitre for five years and then indexed to wholesale prices, which escalation of 12.12 per cent had since taken to ₹ 148; a minimum guaranteed quantity of only 1,800 kilolitres a day; and "Effluent Received", defined in Schedule 4, measured at the common inlet chamber. Lalwani drafted that definition herself, choosing the inlet chamber because it gave one number from one instrument.

Commissioning came in August 2020 at ₹ 64 crore — ₹ 32 crore of central grant under the common effluent treatment plant scheme, ₹ 12.80 crore from the society, ₹ 9.60 crore of equity and ₹ 9.60 crore of term debt. In June 2021, after a National Green Tribunal order on the region's dyeing units, the board tightened its zero-liquid-discharge conditions; Payodhi added a multiple-effect evaporator for ₹ 14 crore, 70 per cent debt-funded, and asked for no tariff increase. Volume, everyone assumed, would reach design capacity by FY2023-24 and pay for it.

3. The industry

India's textile clusters have lived under a zero-liquid-discharge regime since the Supreme Court's orders on the region's dyeing units, and the Central Pollution Control Board has extended that logic across Tamil Nadu. The consequence for an operator like Payodhi is peculiar: the regulated outcome is that nothing leaves the cluster, so the plant is judged on what it recovers while the contract pays it for what it receives. Consent conditions bind the plant, but the load arrives from eighteen independent firms, one of which can undo a quarter's compliance record in a night shift.

The competitor is less another operator than the alternative to a common plant: equipment from Thermax, Ion Exchange and VA Tech Wabag is well understood here, and a mill that can finance ₹ 6 crore of in-house reverse osmosis begins to see the common plant as a tax. Financing runs through SIDBI lines and bank consortia; effluent treatment attracts goods and services tax at 12 per cent. The membrane train is licensed from a Gothenburg process house whose European clients contract on kilograms of salt.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

Until about 2023 the story was simple: volume would grow, the tariff was contractual, and a kilolitre was a kilolitre.

The first crack came from a member's own numbers. Between FY2021-22 and FY2022-23 one of the larger dyeing houses raised its discharge by about a fifth while its inlet strength fell from roughly 7,900 to 4,600 milligrams of dissolved solids a litre. Inder Sadarangani, the plant head, read it at once: borewell water in the drain. Dilution brought it inside the society's house limits, cost almost nothing, and raised Payodhi's invoice — and its power bill, since the evaporator must drive off every litre. The outcome was worse and the revenue better.

The second crack was measurement. In January 2024 the society installed unit-level meters under a state grant, and from FY2024-25 a declared total existed. It has never matched the inlet reading: 2,341 kilolitres a day declared against 2,496 metered in FY2024-25, 2,405 against 2,580 in FY2025-26. Payodhi blames unmetered washdown, stormwater and four meters never recalibrated; the society answers that Payodhi's totaliser sits downstream of the condensate return, so a volume is counted twice.

The third crack came in August 2025, when a complaint and a tribunal-triggered inspection put the board's own totalisers on the permeate and evaporator-feed lines. The board's mass balance caught a stream Schedule 4 does not: the segregated high-TDS line, averaging 132 kilolitres a day, routed past the equalisation tank straight into the recovery train. It is the most expensive water on site and the concession does not pay for it. Sadarangani has also told nobody that the flowmeter was last calibrated by a third party nineteen months ago, with a noted 1.8 per cent drift — on FY2025-26 volumes, 16,951 kilolitres, or ₹ 25.09 lakh in either direction.

5. The people

Poonam Lalwani, 41 — contracts and commercial, Karur

Believes the metric must change and cannot say to what. Her variable pay turns on financial close at Sivakasi, which the lender has tied to Perundurai. She has not told the committee she wrote Schedule 4.

Gopal Vaswani, 58 — managing director and co-founder, Karur

The society signed a per-kilolitre contract and should honour it; reopen the basis once and it reopens every five years. His personal guarantee stands behind ₹ 21.39 crore of group debt. Unmentioned: an August approach from a national water company, which would value a bankable availability contract far more.

Hansa Thadani, 47 — chief financial officer, Karur

Availability, or nothing gets financed: coverage at Perundurai is 1.13 against a covenant of 1.25. She has already run an availability model past the lender's adviser without telling the society.

Inder Sadarangani, 52 — plant head, Perundurai

The only honest measure of the work is dissolved solids removed, and he has the evaporator's power curve. His plant is judged on cost per kilolitre treated, a ratio dilution flatters. He has put neither the calibration drift nor the three members refusing meter access in writing.

Pravin Makhija, 33 — analytics and MIS, Pune

Built Exhibit 2 and refuses to nominate a number; reconciliation, he says, is not a data problem, though he is measured on closing it. Unshared: in 27 of the 52 weeks of FY2025-26 the declared total moved opposite to the inlet meter.

Ghanshyam Hemrajani, 61 — chairman, Ittefaq Dyers' Common Effluent Society

Members will pay for water recovered and returned fit for reuse, the only thing they receive; per kilolitre sent, they pay for the cluster's waste. He faces a society election in March. Unsaid: four of the largest members have ordered in-house reverse osmosis and will need far less returned water.

Karin Wahlström, 49 — process lead, Gothenburg licensor

European operators contract on kilograms of salt removed, and she will underwrite it with a performance guarantee — which is also how she sells membranes. Its clause 9 excludes inlet variability beyond a band the cluster breaches most months.

Hisham Al Dosari, 44 — adviser to the lender consortium, Manama

Lenders fund availability; he will not credit a volume-linked revenue line at more than 70 per cent. He has seen three Indian common plants where availability charges survived the lender and were never collected, and is unsure availability is safer, rather than merely financeable.

7. Voices

"My members send you their problem and you bill them for the size of the problem. When a unit cleans up and sends you less, you earn less — so what are you selling us? Sell us the water back."

Ghanshyam Hemrajani, joint committee pre-meeting, 24 October 2026

"Then in a year when two members bring up their own RO, revenue falls 28.5 per cent and the plant costs the same to run. Row two of Makhija's table: coverage goes negative. I cannot take that to the credit committee, and I cannot take a 1.13 to the auditor."

Hansa Thadani, same meeting

"Salt is the work; water is the vehicle it arrives in. I can weigh salt on a weighbridge in front of anybody. What I cannot do is say which of eighteen units it came from: after the equalisation tank it is one stream and one meter."

Inder Sadarangani, internal note, 19 October 2026

"There is nothing wrong with any of the three. A is an instrument reading on a defined plane. B is a sum of eighteen declarations. C is a mass balance. Asking which is right is like asking whether a room is four metres or twelve square metres."

Pravin Makhija, chat thread from Pune, 29 October 2026

8. The options as Lalwani sees them

Hold Schedule 4 and fix the instruments. Recalibrate, telemeter 41 discharge points for ₹ 161.95 lakh, and invoice the board basis too: ₹ 71.30 lakh a year of unbilled volume, and a revenue line the society understands — while Payodhi still earns more when the cluster behaves worse. Three members have refused meter access.

Charge per kilolitre recovered and returned. Hemrajani's proposal, at ₹ 159.43 per kilolitre with a take-or-pay floor. It prices what the member receives and matches the regulated outcome, but makes revenue a function of members' capital spending and of rainfall; Exhibit 4 shows what that does to coverage.

Charge per kilogram of dissolved solids removed. Sadarangani's and Wahlström's metric, at ₹ 24.83 a kilogram. It tracks the plant's cost almost exactly and rises in the downside case. It is also the only candidate that cannot be allocated between eighteen members from existing instrumentation, and the load itself is contested to 8.59 per cent.

Move to an availability charge. ₹ 116.14 lakh a month for a plant meeting consent limits: bankable, Sivakasi-enabling, covenant-friendly. It pays the same whether the plant treats 2,580 kilolitres a day or nothing, which the society will not sign and which the board's regional officer calls a structure that removes the operator's reason to care.

Move to an outcome charge. A base plus a bonus for each month the cluster's combined discharge meets the board's criteria. It prices what the regulator and the courts care about, and hands Payodhi's marginal earnings to the night-shift discipline of eighteen independent firms, two of them repeat slug-dischargers.

Lalwani has written all five on one page four times, and two doubts keep returning. Every option assumes one metric for one contract, when members range from 430 kilolitres a day at 7,400 milligrams a litre to units a tenth that size at far lower strength. And perhaps the argument is not about the unit at all but about who carries the risk that the unit cannot be measured — which nothing on her page allocates.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The Article 18.4 notice opened a sixty-day window closing 14 December 2026; failing agreement, the basis goes to expert determination, binding for the remaining nine years. The board's protocol is due 15 November and the consent to operate expires 31 December, as does the lender's term sheet for Sivakasi's ₹ 34 crore, which is conditional on an amendment at Perundurai; Al Dosari has said 70 per cent, which no option delivers as drafted. The 1.25 covenant is tested on 31 March 2027 against a current 1.13. The society withholds ₹ 47.27 lakh; the auditor has carried an emphasis of matter on the ₹ 165.84 lakh measurement uncertainty. The minimum guaranteed quantity of 1,800 kilolitres a day is worth ₹ 972.36 lakh a year, ₹ 101.64 lakh below cash operating cost before any debt service, so the floor negotiated in 2019 protects nothing that matters. Any change of basis needs the society's general body, the lender and the consent application: three counterparties, three calendars, one plant.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 2 and 3, state what each reading measures. Are any of them wrong, and if not, what was the contract supposed to count?
  2. Take each candidate in Exhibit 4. What does it reward in the member, what in the operator, and where does the reward part from the board's outcome?
  3. Exhibit 4's rates are back-solved from the invoiced ₹ 1,393.72 lakh. What does Exhibit 2 do to every figure in it?
  4. Exhibit 6 shows most of the annual cash requirement is fixed. Does that argue for an availability charge, or only a fixed component inside another metric?
  5. Al Dosari, Wahlström and Hemrajani each want a different metric, for sound reasons. Whose interest best aligns with the plant surviving to 2035, and how would you test that on Exhibit 5?
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Lalwani table at half past ten, what does she decline to table, and what does she tell the board in December if the society and the lender cannot both be satisfied?

At a quarter past midnight she wrote one line at the foot of the page she had not printed: we have been selling a measurement, not a service, and the measurement is the thing nobody agrees on. Then she crossed it out, having nothing to put in its place before half past ten.

Chamak Linen Services: Deciding What to Charge Per

A decision case on the value metric in commercial laundry and linen rental

1. Opening

On Tuesday, 6 October 2026, Chaitanya Gaonkar, chief executive of Chamak Linen Services, sat in a first-floor meeting room in Panaji with a printed spreadsheet and a cup of tea gone cold. The Goa season began within a month, and on 1 November 96 of the company's 212 hotel and hospital contracts came up for renewal. Renewal letters had to go out by 31 October, and each had to say what Chamak charged per what.

For fifteen years the answer had been a rate per kilogram of linen washed. Chaitanya now suspected that this simplicity was costing money and irritating the best customers.

2. Company background

Chamak Linen Services was founded in 2011 by Chaitanya's father in a rented shed in Vasco da Gama. Today it runs two plants, Vasco da Gama (about 14 tonnes of linen a day) and Mapusa (about 6 tonnes), and a Karwar depot for coastal hospitals. With about 640 staff, it serves 140 hotels and resorts and 72 hospitals and nursing homes. Revenue is about ₹ 3.2 crore a month, or about ₹ 38 crore a year, at a rate of ₹ 60 per kilogram.

Competition comes from small regional laundry contractors who undercut on price and from the in-house laundries of chains such as Taj and Lemon Tree. Hospital groups such as Manipal and Apollo set infection-control expectations that smaller hospitals must meet for NABH accreditation. Chamak's water use and effluent are governed by consent from the Goa State Pollution Control Board, which effectively caps how much it can wash at Vasco da Gama.

3. The situation

Three things had gone wrong with the kilogram. First, hotels had learned to shrink it. Over eighteen months, three large properties replaced heavy towels with lighter ones and cut their weight per room-night by about a tenth. Their bills fell by the same tenth, though the pieces Chamak sorted, folded and delivered did not change. Second, hospital linen is heavy, soiled and needs thermal disinfection, so a kilogram from a ward costs far more to process than a kilogram from a hotel, yet both are billed at ₹ 60. Third, customers disputed weights, since wet and dry kilograms differ.

Trupti Parab, an analyst in Pune, assembled Exhibit 1 from five representative accounts. Cost to serve differs sharply: ₹ 42 a kilogram for the resort and business hotel, ₹ 51 for hospital work, and ₹ 63 for the boutique hotel, where small lots and hand finishing dominate.

The wider team saw the problem from different places. Yusuf Al Balushi, who runs procurement for a Muscat hotel group that had asked Chamak for advice on its Goa property, said Gulf hotels rarely buy laundry by weight; they buy it per occupied room, the number their owners understand. Thandi Mokoena, a linen-systems consultant in Cape Town, had seen hospital groups there move to per-piece pricing once garments carried RFID chips, and warned that pieces are fair only if the list reflects the different effort behind a mat and a surgical gown.

4. The people

Chaitanya Gaonkar, chief executive, Panaji. He wants a metric explainable in one sentence that keeps the best accounts.

Lourdes Fernandes, chief financial officer, Panaji. She wants margin that does not swing with the tourist calendar, and fears disputes over customer-reported data.

Tanvi Sardessai, head of operations, Vasco da Gama. Her costs follow kilograms, which drive water, steam and chemicals, and pieces, which drive sorting and finishing labour. She wants no reward for light linen.

Yashwant Volvoikar, head of key accounts, Margao. He carries the renewal targets and fears that any change will hand rivals an excuse to pitch.

5. Exhibits

Four metrics were modelled on the five accounts: today's ₹ 60 per kilogram, ₹ 20 per piece, ₹ 280 per occupied room-night or bed-day, and a fixed fee of ₹ 6,000 per available room or bed. Exhibit 2 shows what each customer would pay; Exhibit 3 shows Chamak's margin after the costs in Exhibit 1.

No metric is neutral for every customer. Per piece or per room-night, the resort and the business hotel pay 17 to 56 per cent more, while the hospital and nursing home pay less. In Exhibit 3 the hospital's ₹ 2,67,300 margin exists only because heavy linen is billed by weight; per piece or per room-night it falls to a small loss, so a flat rate is wrong for hospitals. The fixed fee gives the lowest total margin and a ₹ 1,08,180 loss on the nursing home.

Seasonality matters as much. The 200-room resort runs at 90 per cent occupancy from November to February, 68 per cent in the shoulder months and 46 per cent in the monsoon, averaging 68 per cent. In a monsoon month it washes 11,040 kg, worth ₹ 6,62,400 at ₹ 60. Under a fixed fee it would still pay ₹ 12,00,000, which is 81.2 per cent more, and Yashwant expected it to walk. Per room-night the same month costs ₹ 7,72,800, so the bill follows the hotel's own revenue.

6. The options

Option 1: keep the kilogram and repair it. Retain ₹ 60 per kilogram but weigh linen dry on calibrated scales and add a clause for lightweight fabrics. The upside is that nothing changes for customers. The cost is that price stays tied to weight while labour is tied to pieces.

Option 2: a piece-rate card. Price each item, from pillowcase to blanket, on a card averaging ₹ 20. The upside is that price follows handling effort. The cost is a long card to negotiate and the result in Exhibit 2: rises of 25 and 33 per cent for the resort and business hotel, while the hospital still loses money.

Option 3: per occupied room-night or bed-day, with rate bands. Charge per occupied room-night or bed-day, taken from the hotel's night-audit report or the hospital's daily census, at a rate set by linen specification. The upside is that the customer pays for what it sells and Chamak's revenue moves with the customer's. The cost is dependence on customer occupancy data and explaining why hotels pay different rates.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, what drives Chamak's cost to serve each account, and how does each candidate unit track it?
  2. Using Exhibits 2 and 3, who wins and loses under each metric, and whom can Chamak least afford to lose?
  3. What does each customer control under each metric, and what behaviour does it encourage?
  4. Which option would you take to Yashwant's meeting, and how would you price hospitals and hotels differently?

8. A note for the learner

The value metric is the unit on which the price is charged, and the test is simple: the price should rise when the customer gets more value, and fall when it gets less. A metric customers can shrink without changing the work Chamak does, as hotels did with lighter towels, fails it. Exhibit 3 shows a second lesson: total margin barely moves with the metric, only who pays it.

One defensible path is Option 3, banded. A hotel's value from laundry is a clean room on every night it sells; a hospital's is safe linen on every occupied bed. Both are counted in occupied room-nights or bed-days, which the customer cannot game with lighter fabric. Bands answer the objection that accounts differ. A suggested card is ₹ 185 for lean linen (up to 3.5 kg per room-night), ₹ 240 for standard (3.5 to 4.5), ₹ 320 for heavy (over 4.5) and ₹ 340 for clinical linen in hospitals.

On the five accounts this yields a bill of ₹ 40,13,280, which is 1.2 per cent above today's ₹ 39,65,940, and a margin of ₹ 8,35,227 against ₹ 7,87,887. Bills move by 0.0 per cent (resort), +2.8 (business hotel), +3.0 (hospital), +6.7 (boutique hotel) and -5.6 (nursing home), so no account faces a shock and the hospital earns a positive margin. Disputes are limited by monthly reconciliation to night-audit and census reports. Roll it out first to the 96 contracts renewing on 1 November, and keep the kilogram for small accounts that cannot supply occupancy data.
